note.note:
History:
• 46-year-old woman presents with progressive numbness and tingling of the left upper extremity.  
• Onset: ≈2 weeks ago, shortly after starting a boxing class.  
• Course: Initially mild tingling in left hand; now constant numbness from elbow to hand with subjective weakness.  
• Distribution: Palmar aspect of 2nd-4th digits; occasional involvement of elbow and shoulder discomfort on movement.  
• Aggravating/relieving: Not improved with massage, warm baths, or ibuprofen.  
• Associated symptoms: One transient (≈20 min) episode of partial visual loss in left eye a few weeks ago; intermittent “fatigue-type” headaches; denies seizures, lower-limb weakness.  
• No confirmed neck pain (patient both affirmed and denied – conflict noted).  
• Jaw pain typed in pre-visit questionnaire but not pursued during interview.  
• Functional impact: Difficulty with piano playing; occasional object handling difficulty.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• Recent upper-respiratory illness (“bad cold/flu”) one month ago lasting ~2 weeks.  
• Allergies: Not recorded.  
• Current medications: Ibuprofen PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented); vitamin D (dose/freq ND); iron supplement occasionally (dose/freq ND); melatonin occasionally (dose/freq ND).  

Family History:
• Father – hypothyroidism, unspecified autoimmune condition.  
• Mother – type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia.  
• No known familial neurologic disorders.  

Social/Functional History (from transcript):
• Right-hand dominant; physically active; recently started boxing class.  
• Occasional heavy alcohol use reported; smoking/drug history not discussed.  

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consultation only; no vitals recorded.  
• General: Alert, oriented, conversational.  
• Cranial nerves/vision: Subjectively normal at time of visit; no exam performed.  
• Motor/sensory: Patient-reported numbness and subjective weakness in left arm; no objective testing documented.  
• Gait/lower limbs: Patient reports normal walking.  
• Neck: No exam findings; presence of pain uncertain (conflicting patient statements).  

Impression:
Progressive unilateral (left) upper-limb sensory deficit with transient unilateral visual disturbance — concerning for a central demyelinating process such as multiple sclerosis; alternative peripheral/structural causes (cervical radiculopathy, median nerve entrapment) remain possible.

Top aligned differentials (consistent with transcript):
1. Multiple sclerosis – separate neurologic episodes (visual loss, limb paresthesia) in a middle-aged woman with recent viral illness and family autoimmune background.  
2. Cervical radiculopathy (C6/C7) – arm/hand distribution possibly precipitated by repetitive boxing activity.  
3. Median nerve entrapment – palmar 2nd-4th digit involvement, but proximal symptoms less typical.

Management Plan:
• Urgent neurology referral initiated for comprehensive evaluation and MRI brain/spine.  
• No disease-specific treatment begun; patient informed that management (e.g., steroids) depends on confirmed diagnosis.  
• Safety-net advice: Attend emergency department if weakness spreads to legs, new or worsening headaches, vomiting, seizures, or recurrent/worsening visual loss.  
• Continue usual OTC analgesia for unrelated musculoskeletal discomfort only as needed.  
• Encourage moderation of boxing activity until diagnosis established.

Patient Summary:
46-year-old woman with a 2-week history of progressive numbness/weakness in the left arm and a prior brief visual-field loss in the same eye is being urgently referred to neurology to rule out multiple sclerosis or other neurologic pathology. No acute treatment started; red-flag advice provided.

Key Takeaways:
• Monitor for any rapid progression (leg weakness, persistent vision changes, severe headache) and seek immediate care if these occur.  
• Await neurology appointment and MRI; no steroids or new medications until diagnosis confirmed.  

Next Steps:
• Neurology clinic appointment – urgent (within 2 weeks) with MRI brain/spinal cord ± visual evoked potentials.  
• Consider formal neurological examination and cervical imaging if peripheral lesion suspected.  
• Update primary care provider with referral details and ensure follow-up once results available.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing elements: vital signs, allergy status confirmation, complete medication doses/frequencies, objective neurological exam, social history (smoking/drugs), menstrual/reproductive history.  
• Conflicts: Patient both affirmed and denied neck pain; jaw pain mentioned in intake but not discussed further.  
• Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor overlapping speech and one ambiguous response regarding neck pain.
